paras: The lynching of Ed Turner took place on the night of Saturday, March 12, 1881, at Mississippi City in Harrison County, Mississippi, when a party of fifty or sixty armed and masked men took Turner, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Turner was being held on an accusation that he had raped a white woman, Mrs. Mike McIntosh. Mississippi and Tennessee papers reported local approval of the killing, and a short telegraphic account ran from California to New Hampshire.

According to a Handsboro dispatch to the Memphis Daily Appeal, Mrs. McIntosh was "a white lady" living on Wolf River near Pass Christian in Harrison County, and the alleged assault took place on the 5th. Wire versions of the story dated the assault March 6 and called it "an outrage" or a gross assault. Turner was confined in the jail at Mississippi City; none of the reports describe his arrest or any statement by him.

At about 11 o'clock on Saturday night a party of fifty or sixty men came to the jail. The Memphis Appeal described them as armed, while the New Orleans Democrat's special and the Jackson Weekly Clarion described them as masked. Rather than have the jail doors broken down with axes, the jailer gave up the keys. The men took Turner out and hanged him to an oak tree near Le Garden hotel, which the Democrat's correspondent placed half a mile from the jail.

Coroner J. T. Baldwin impaneled a jury, but the body was not taken down until 3 o'clock in the afternoon, "owing to some misunderstanding of the law in the premises." The Clarion's dispatch of Sunday, March 13, said the coroner's jury took the body down that evening. No verdict of the coroner's jury, arrest, or grand jury action appears in the coverage. Instead, the Appeal's correspondent wrote that "the action of the lynchers meets the approval of all good citizens," and the Clarion's that "the people approve the lynching."

The fullest accounts came from Southern papers, which framed the killing as deserved punishment. The Memphis Daily Appeal ran its dispatch on March 16 under the headline "A Ravisher Meets His Deservings at the Hands of an Infuriated Mob," and the Jackson Weekly Clarion of March 17 headed its special "A Scoundrel Gets His Deserts. A Negro Ravisher Hung at Mississippi City." Both papers stated the rape accusation as fact and called Turner a "ravisher."

Outside Mississippi the story spread mainly through two telegrams. A one-sentence Handsboro wire dated March 13 appeared the next day in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union under "Hanged by a Mob" and in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer under "Another One Lynched." A longer special to the New Orleans Democrat, which added the number of men and the distance from the jail, ran on March 14 and 15 in the Alexandria Gazette, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle and the Savannah Morning News, the last under "Negro Lynched in Mississippi." The People and New Hampshire Patriot printed a version of the same special on March 17 that placed the lynching on Sunday night.

Through late March and early April, weekly papers reduced the story to a line among other crime news. The South Kentuckian wrote that "Ed Turner Col." was lynched at "Hindsboro" for "grossly assaulting" Mrs. McIntosh, the Batesville Guard, the Iron County Register and the Iola Register printed that Turner "committed an indecent assault upon a white woman," and the New Ulm Weekly Review said "the people of Mississippi City" had lynched him. Like the wire reports, these briefs repeated the accusation as established fact.

Reports differ on the date of the alleged assault, which the Memphis Appeal gave as the 5th and the wire reports as March 6. The New Hampshire Patriot's "Sunday night" conflicts with the Saturday night given by the Appeal and the Democrat's special, and with Handsboro dispatches dated Sunday, March 13, which said Turner was taken "last night." The place of the hanging appears as an oak near Le Garden hotel in the Appeal, a tree half a mile from the jail in the Democrat's special, and a tree "near" the jail in the Clarion.

Turner was hanged by fifty or sixty men who forced the jail keys from the jailer, with no legal proceeding, to punish an alleged assault on a white woman (A7, A5); the papers called the killers 'lynchers' and a mob (A7, A1).

Three separately sourced dispatches from Handsboro (the short wire in A1/A2, the New Orleans Democrat special in A5, and the specials to the Memphis Appeal and Jackson Clarion in A7 and A9) agree that Turner was taken from the Mississippi City jail and hanged.
